newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FOCUS-Slovak trade gap widens, seen accelerating.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Slovak trade gap widens, seen accelerating.

text.p: Slovakia's trade deficit yawned wider in the first five months of this year and analysts warned on Wednesday that faster growth of imports over exports will impede a return to the black.

The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) said that foreign trade gap rose to 29.859 billion crowns in the 1997 January-May period, from 27.908 billion crowns in the first four months of this year. This compares with a 25.674 billion crown gap in the first five months of 1996.
"The deficit continues to widen which itself is a bad sign. But most worrying is that (the growth of) imports are still outpacing exports," said Vladimir Kuklis of Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka.
SUSR said imports during the reported period totalled 149.117 billion crowns, a year-on-year rise of 13.8 percent, while exports totalled 119.257 billion crowns, up 13.2 percent.
"Faster import dynamics indicate that it will be difficult to reverse the yawn in the trade deficit," said another Bratislava-based foreign analyst.
"Furthemore it can easily put the central bank's target of a current account deficit of five percent of full year GDP out of reach", he added.

Government officials have repeatedly said the full year trade deficit should not exceed last year's gap of 64.5 billion crowns, which, still would still represent roughly 10 percent of the projected GDP.
Analysts said both the central bank (NBS) and the government had only few tools to curb rising imports.
"The NBS cannnot limit credit expansion much further, while the government has few measures at its disposal to curb imports without being too protectionist," said Kuklis.
The NBS last summer imposed tight monetary measures to limit rapidly growing credit expansion which fuelled consumer imports.
The government is to introduce a series of measures aimed at limiting imports including a law against excessively subsidised goods and dumped imports.
It is also launching an Export-Import bank and creating a special fund to boost Slovak exports.
"I would not be too optimistic," said Kuklis. "Both the Exim bank and the pro-export fund will only show a first positive effect after some five years, if at all."
Another trade problem looming on the horizon may be the slowing in sales of steel and steel products which remain Slovakia's main export articles.
Exports of steel and steel products totalled 26.374 billion crowns in the January-May period, up 3.3 percent year-on-year.
"It seems that the steel industry, generating a large portion of our exports, has reached its ceiling. These exports will probably not show any radical increase later this year," said Kuklis.
